questions_and_answers.question_text: Which words are used for "from" with people, and which with places?
When can cóng be followed by a person?
What does ràng mean when followed by a person and an adjectival verb?
What did you learn ràng to mean in the Welfare module?
Write the Chinese for "I went and tried to borrow it, but I didn't get it."

answers.answer_text: Wǒ qù jièguo, kěshi méi jièdào.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "I borrowed five dollars from him."

answers.answer_text: Wǒ cóng tā nàr jièle wǔkuài qián.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Give the pattern for borrowing from a person using wèn.

answers.answer_text: Wèn...jiè... — literally "ask...borrow...", as in Wǒ wèn ta jièle yìběn shū.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "What he said made me very angry."

answers.answer_text: Tā shuōde huà ràng wǒ hěn shēngqì.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Does jiè by itself imply that the thing was obtained?

answers.answer_text: No — jiè by itself does not necessarily imply obtaining.

articles.text:
1. A: Jīntian wǒ jièdào yìběn hǎo    Today I borrowed a good novel
      xiǎoshuō.                       (from someone).
   B: Shénme xiǎoshuō, ràng ni       What novel is it that makes you
      zènme gāoxìng?                  so happy?

Notes on No. 1

jiè: "to borrow" (Also "to lend"; see Notes on No. 2.)

Wǒ dào túshūguǎn qù jiè shū.     I'm going to the library to borrow
                                 (take out) some books.

For "from," use gēn or xiàng for people and cóng for place names like the library.

Wǒ méi dài qián, xiǎng gēn       I didn't bring any money. I want to
Níngning qù jiè.                 go borrow some from Níngning.
Wǒ cóng túshūguǎn jièle yìběn    I borrowed a Chinese history book
Zhōngguo lìshǐ shū.              from the library.

Cóng can only be followed by a person if the person is made into a place name, for example by the addition of nǎr (nàli):

Wǒ cóng tā nàr jièle wǔkuài      I borrowed five dollars from him.
qián.

For people, you may also use the common pattern wèn...jiè..., literally "ask...borrow...":

Wǒ wèn ta jièle yìběn shū.       I borrowed a book from him.
Wǒ bù hǎo yìsi wèn biérén jiè    I'm too embarrassed to borrow money
qián.                            from other people.

jièdào: The ending -dào expresses that the borrowing results in the thing being obtained. Jiè by itself does not necessarily imply obtaining, so you can use it in situations when you tried to borrow something but couldn't get it.

Wǒ gēn ta jièle yìběn zìdiǎn.    I borrowed a dictionary from him.
Wǒ qù jièguo, kěshi méi jièdào.  I went and tried to borrow it, but
                                 I didn't get it.

Jiè may have certain other directional or resultative endings:

Zài zhèr kàn kěyi, bù néng       You can read it here, but you can't
jièchuqu.                        take it out.
Tā bǎ wǒde chē jièqu le.         He borrowed my car (and took it away).
Wǒ cóng tā nàr jièlai wǔkuài     I borrowed five dollars from him.
qián.

ràng: "to make" someone a certain way, or "to cause" someone to become a certain way. When used this way, ràng is followed by a person and an adjectival verb. You learned ràng as "to let" in the Welfare module.

Tā shuōde huà ràng wǒ hěn        What he said made me very angry.
shēngqì.
Tā nàme bú kèqi ràng tā          He embarrassed his friend by being
péngyou hěn bù hǎo yìsi.         so rude.

Shénme xiǎoshuō?--ràng ni zhème gāoxìng: There is a pause after the question shénme xiǎoshuō, and the rest of the sentence is like an afterthought.

Zhèi shi shénme kāfēi?--zhème    What kind of coffee is this? It's
hǎo hē.                          so good.
Nǐ xǐhuan shùxué a?--nàme méi    You like math?--such a boring thing!
yìsi!
